entry.title: Should wallets default to Taproot or SegWit receive addresses while some services still reject bc1p?
entry.summary:
Taproot was designed to provide tangible benefits to all Bitcoin users, not just those leveraging advanced script functionality. The core innovation behind Taproot is the introduction of a unified output type that seamlessly serves both direct payments to public keys and more complex scripts. This consolidation results in transaction structures that are typically more cost-efficient than earlier alternatives. Additionally, Taproot incentivizes privacy-preserving techniques by allowing solutions that mask their internal policies on-chain, as long as transactions utilize the key path spend. This approach means that wallet activities, whether simple or complex, become indistinguishable from each other, contributing to broader anonymity.
For everyday users, especially those relying on straightforward wallets, Taproot offers two main advantages: lower transaction fees and enhanced policy privacy. By sharing an anonymity set that includes even non-simple wallets, Taproot ensures that simple transactions do not stand out on the blockchain. However, these benefits remain limited while overall adoption is low—a situation reminiscent of the chicken-and-egg dilemma. Until sending to P2TR addresses becomes universally supported, there are valid concerns about making Taproot the default for receiving funds. Furthermore, while inputs become cheaper with Taproot, outputs are slightly more expensive, which means the fee savings can vary depending on the transaction’s structure, particularly for users who generate many change outputs.
Concerns regarding post-quantum (PQ) threats have also been raised in discussions about Taproot adoption. However, continuing to use legacy formats like P2WPKH or P2WSH does not offer any extra protection against potential PQ vulnerabilities, since public keys and related information are already widely exposed within Bitcoin’s ecosystem. The cryptographic system intentionally treats this data as public, and numerous software implementations depend on this characteristic.
Although it is important to consider the trade-offs and acknowledge current limitations in adoption and infrastructure support, the technical and privacy improvements introduced by Taproot justify recommending its use as the default. The move toward greater Taproot adoption aligns with Bitcoin’s goals of efficiency, privacy, and future readiness.
